title: Sylvester's Sequence: Telescoping Reciprocal Sums and Pairwise Coprimality
description: Sylvester's sequence a₀=2, a_{n+1}=aₙ²-aₙ+1 (2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, …) has two classical elementary properties, both fully machine-checked here with 0 sorries and 0 axioms. (1) Closed-form partial reciprocal sums: ∑_{k≤n} 1/aₖ = 1 - 1/(a_{n+1}-1), so the infinite reciprocal sum equals 1 — an explicit Egyptian-fraction representation of unity. (2) Pairwise coprimality of distinct terms, via the Euclid-style product formula a_{n+1} = (∏_{k≤n} aₖ) + 1. The engine is the telescoping identity 1/aₙ = 1/(aₙ-1) - 1/(a_{n+1}-1), which follows from a_{n+1}-1 = aₙ(aₙ-1).

meta.author: James Joseph Sylvester (1880)
meta.assumptions: None. The sequence is defined directly in ℕ; all results are proved from the recurrence with no axioms and no structure-encoded hypotheses.
originalContributions: Closed-form partial reciprocal sum syl_partial_sum: ∑_{k≤n} 1/aₖ = 1 - 1/(a_{n+1}-1), proved by induction using the telescoping per-term identity
Telescoping identity syl_recip_term: 1/aₙ = 1/(aₙ-1) - 1/(a_{n+1}-1), the algebraic heart of the result
Euclid-style product formula syl_eq_prod_add_one: a_{n+1} = (∏_{k≤n} aₖ) + 1
Pairwise coprimality syl_coprime: distinct terms share no common factor, derived from the product formula
prerequisites: Elementary divisibility and gcd in ℕ

overview.historicalContext: Sylvester's sequence is named for James Joseph Sylvester, who studied it in 1880 in connection with Egyptian fractions — sums of distinct unit fractions $1/n$ used by the ancient Egyptians (the Rhind papyrus, c. 1650 BCE) to represent rationals. The sequence is the *greedy* solution to expanding $1$ as a sum of unit fractions: at each stage subtract the largest $1/m$ that keeps the running total below $1$. Sylvester showed this greedy process is governed by the recurrence $a_{n+1} = a_n^2 - a_n + 1$. The same sequence, in its Euclid-style product form $a_{n+1} = a_0 a_1 \cdots a_n + 1$, reappears in Curtiss's 1922 work on the densest packings of unit fractions and in the theory of Znám's problem and Sasaki's bounds. It is catalogued as OEIS A000058 and grows doubly exponentially, with roughly $\lfloor E^{2^{n+1}} \rfloor$ behavior for Vardi's constant $E \approx 1.2640847$.
overview.problemStatement: Let $a_0 = 2$ and $a_{n+1} = a_n^2 - a_n + 1$, so $a = 2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, 3263443, \dots$. Prove two classical facts. (1) **Closed-form partial sums:** $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{1}{a_k} = 1 - \frac{1}{a_{n+1} - 1}$, so the infinite reciprocal series sums to exactly $1$. (2) **Pairwise coprimality:** for $i \ne j$, $\gcd(a_i, a_j) = 1$.
overview.proofStrategy: Both results flow from the single observation $a_{n+1} - 1 = a_n(a_n - 1)$. For the reciprocal sum, this factorization yields the telescoping per-term identity $\frac{1}{a_n} = \frac{1}{a_n - 1} - \frac{1}{a_{n+1} - 1}$ (proved by clearing denominators with `field_simp` and `ring`, using $a_n \ge 2$ to keep every denominator nonzero); induction then collapses the sum to $1 - \frac{1}{a_{n+1} - 1}$. For coprimality, the same factorization gives the Euclid-style product formula $a_{n+1} = \prod_{k \le n} a_k + 1$; hence every earlier term divides $a_{n+1} - 1$, so a common divisor of $a_i$ and a later $a_j$ would divide both $a_j$ and $a_j - 1$ and therefore divide $1$. A subtlety handled explicitly is $\mathbb{N}$'s truncated subtraction: the recurrence is lifted to $\mathbb{Z}$ (`syl_cast_succ`) before any cancellation, after establishing $a_n \le a_n^2$.
keyInsights: A single algebraic identity, $a_{n+1} - 1 = a_n(a_n - 1)$, simultaneously drives the telescoping reciprocal sum and the Euclid product formula — the two famous properties are two faces of one factorization.

The reciprocals of Sylvester's sequence form an Egyptian-fraction representation of $1$ with an *exact* error term: truncating at $n$ leaves precisely $1/(a_{n+1} - 1)$, so the partial sums approach $1$ doubly exponentially fast.

The product formula $a_{n+1} = a_0 \cdots a_n + 1$ is literally Euclid's infinitude-of-primes construction applied recursively, which is why distinct terms are automatically coprime and why each term supplies a fresh prime factor.
Pairwise coprimality reduces to the elementary fact that any common divisor of $N$ and $N-1$ divides their difference $1$ — coprimality here needs no prime factorization, only divisibility.

Working in $\mathbb{N}$ forces care with truncated subtraction: the proof first proves $a_n \ge 2$, then lifts the recurrence to $\mathbb{Z}$ so that ring normalization is valid without underflow side conditions.

mainTheorems.name: syl_partial_sum
mainTheorems.description: Closed form for the partial sums of reciprocals. Because a_{n+1} - 1 grows without bound, the infinite series of reciprocals converges to exactly 1.

mainTheorems.name: syl_recip_term
mainTheorems.description: The telescoping per-term identity that drives the partial-sum formula, a consequence of a_{n+1} - 1 = aₙ(aₙ - 1).

mainTheorems.name: syl_eq_prod_add_one
mainTheorems.description: Euclid-style product formula: each term is one more than the product of all previous terms.

mainTheorems.name: syl_coprime
mainTheorems.description: Distinct terms of the sequence are coprime, since aᵢ divides aⱼ - 1 while also any common factor divides aⱼ.

sections.title: Imports and Module Docstring
sections.summary: `import Mathlib`, the module docstring, and `namespace SylvesterSequenceOQ01`. The docstring fixes Sylvester's sequence (a₀ = 2, a_{n+1} = aₙ² − aₙ + 1; 2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, …), states the two machine-checked results — the closed-form partial reciprocal sum and pairwise coprimality — and names the engine: the telescoping identity 1/aₙ = 1/(aₙ−1) − 1/(a_{n+1}−1), valid because a_{n+1} − 1 = aₙ(aₙ − 1).

sections.title: The Sequence and Basic Bounds
sections.summary: Defines syl by structural recursion (a₀ = 2, a_{n+1} = aₙ² - aₙ + 1), exposes the base case and recurrence as rewrite lemmas, proves two_le_syl (every term ≥ 2), and lifts the recurrence to ℤ via syl_cast_succ to avoid ℕ's truncated subtraction.
sections.mathContext: $a_n \ge 2$ for all $n$; the $\mathbb{Z}$-lift $a_{n+1}=a_n^2-a_n+1$ removes $\mathbb{N}$ truncated subtraction.

sections.title: Telescoping Identity and Closed-Form Reciprocal Sum
sections.summary: Proves the per-term telescoping identity syl_recip_term (1/aₙ = 1/(aₙ-1) - 1/(a_{n+1}-1)) from the factorization a_{n+1}-1 = aₙ(aₙ-1), then inducts to obtain the closed form syl_partial_sum: ∑_{k≤n} 1/aₖ = 1 - 1/(a_{n+1}-1), whence the infinite sum equals 1.

sections.title: Euclid Product Formula and Divisibility Bridge
sections.summary: Establishes the Euclid-style product formula syl_eq_prod_add_one (a_{n+1} = ∏_{k≤n} aₖ + 1) by induction using the recurrence, then derives the divisibility bridge syl_dvd_succ_sub_one: for i ≤ n, aᵢ divides a_{n+1} − 1, because aᵢ appears as a factor of the product ∏_{k≤n} aₖ = a_{n+1} − 1.
sections.mathContext: $a_{n+1} = \Big(\prod_{k\le n} a_k\Big) + 1 \Rightarrow a_i \mid a_{n+1}-1$ for $i \le n$.

sections.title: Pairwise Coprimality of Distinct Terms
sections.summary: Concludes syl_coprime: distinct terms aᵢ, aⱼ (i < j) are coprime. Writing j = i + n + 1, the divisibility bridge gives aᵢ ∣ aⱼ − 1; any common divisor d of aᵢ and aⱼ then divides both aⱼ and aⱼ − 1, hence divides their difference 1, so gcd(aᵢ, aⱼ) = 1.
sections.mathContext: $d \mid a_j$ and $d \mid a_j-1 \Rightarrow d \mid 1$, so $\gcd(a_i,a_j)=1$ for $i<j$.

crossReferences.description: Sylvester's product formula $a_{n+1} = a_0 \cdots a_n + 1$ is exactly Euclid's infinitude-of-primes construction applied recursively; pairwise coprimality of the terms gives a second proof that infinitely many primes exist.
Where the harmonic series $\sum 1/n$ diverges, Sylvester's reciprocals $\sum 1/a_k$ converge — to exactly $1$ — because the terms grow doubly exponentially rather than linearly.
Both compute an exact closed value for a series of reciprocals; here the sum of $1/a_k$ equals $1$, an Egyptian-fraction unit, rather than the Basel value $\pi^2/6$.
Perfect numbers are characterized by their unit-fraction divisor sums; Sylvester's sequence is the greedy unit-fraction expansion of $1$, a neighboring topic in the arithmetic of reciprocals.

conclusion.summary: Two elementary but elegant facts about Sylvester's sequence are fully machine-checked with zero sorries and zero axioms. First, the reciprocals telescope to an exact closed form $\sum_{k\le n} 1/a_k = 1 - 1/(a_{n+1}-1)$, so the infinite reciprocal series is an Egyptian-fraction representation of $1$. Second, distinct terms are pairwise coprime. Both rest on the single factorization $a_{n+1} - 1 = a_n(a_n - 1)$, which yields the telescoping identity on one hand and the Euclid product formula $a_{n+1} = \prod_{k\le n} a_k + 1$ on the other.
conclusion.implications: The formalization captures, in a few elementary lemmas, why Sylvester's sequence is the canonical example linking greedy Egyptian-fraction expansions to Euclid's coprimality argument. The exact error term $1/(a_{n+1}-1)$ exhibits the fastest-possible greedy convergence to $1$, and pairwise coprimality means each term contributes a new prime, recovering the infinitude of primes. The proof also illustrates the standard discipline for natural-number recurrences: prove the no-underflow bound, then lift to ℤ before any cancellation.
openQuestions: Can the convergence be promoted to a formal Tendsto statement, $\sum_{k\le n} 1/a_k \to 1$, by combining the closed form with $a_{n+1} - 1 \to \infty$?
Is there a clean Lean formalization of Vardi's closed form $a_n = \lfloor E^{2^{n+1}} + 1/2 \rfloor$ for the doubly-exponential constant $E$, linking the recurrence to a single real parameter?
Does the greedy/Euclid product structure generalize to a formalized treatment of Znám's problem, where one seeks sets with $a_i \mid \prod_{j\ne i} a_j + 1$?
